about: One entry per experiment, the source of Discord's #experiments channel. experiments.md keeps the detailed record; whenever an experiment is added there or its status or result changes, update its entry here in the same step. Times are Toronto time, like "Oct 18, 6:55 AM". status: planned, running, deploying, done-kept, done-reverted, closed.

experiments.title: Strict gate, human-game starts, extra targets, 400 searches
experiments.what: Self-play used 400 searches per move (was 160), started 25% of games from positions in people's games, and a strict promotion gate judged each new net.
experiments.why: Better training targets should give nets that clearly beat round 19 and predict live games better.
experiments.metric: Promotions over rounds 23-26, and the live value error falling below about 0.63.
experiments.result: 1 promotion in 4 matches (round 24, 54.2% ± 3.2% over 900 games); scores 49.9 / 54.2 / 50.5 / 50.8%. Live value error stayed at 0.635-0.638. Kept: no sign of harm, and it gave the one promotion.

experiments.title: Model of people's moves inside the search (Petra, bot5)
experiments.what: On bot5 only, the search predicts the opponent's moves with a model trained on people's moves, not with the bot's own policy.
experiments.why: Search that expects human moves could exploit human habits and resist repeat opponents.
experiments.metric: bot5's ranked win rate against bot3 and bot4 over the same hours, at 400 games.
experiments.result: No effect shown: bot5 278-205 over 483 games (57.6%, 53.1-61.9%) against 57.4% for the controls. The model stays on bot5; no rollout.

experiments.title: Fresh human data every round
experiments.what: Before each round, the newest live games are added to training: value positions, game starts, and a refreshed model of people's moves.
experiments.why: Learning from the newest live games should keep the live value error falling.
experiments.metric: Live value error trend and the people's-move model's held-out accuracy, rounds 24-27.
experiments.result: Runs reliably, so it stays on. No learning gain shown: same-holdout error 0.640 vs 0.644, and the people's-move model flat (64.9% vs 65.2%).

experiments.title: A shorter, fresher training window
experiments.what: Training uses the last 6 rounds of self-play (was 8), drops the old pre-graph-net games, and repeats people's games 4 times (was 10).
experiments.why: The new 400-search games were only about 10% of what each net learned from.
experiments.metric: Promotions and mean match score over rounds 27-30 against rounds 22-26; live value error must not rise.
experiments.result: 2 promotions in 4 rounds (55.8%, 50.1%, 50.8%, 53.5%) against E1's 1 in 4. Live value error flat (0.627 vs 0.625). Kept.

experiments.title: 35% of self-play games start from people's games
experiments.what: Raised the share of self-play games that start from a position in a human game from 25% to 35%.
experiments.why: More training from human-like positions could improve decisions in live games, especially early.
experiments.metric: Promotions and same-holdout live value error, rounds 32-43.
experiments.result: Inconclusive. One promotion (round 40) in 12 rounds; the value error changes all crossed zero (round 40: -0.002, interval -0.008 to +0.005). 35% stays as the baseline, not as a proven gain.

experiments.title: Share self-play games by each worker's measured speed
experiments.what: Self-play games are split between machines by each one's measured games per second, not by its number of processes.
experiments.why: The slow PC was getting the biggest share and held up the end of every round.
experiments.metric: Self-play time per round against rounds 29-30, with exactly 3,500 games and no gaps.
experiments.result: Self-play fell from 86 min (round 31) to about 46 min (rounds 32-39), 3,500 games every round. Kept.

experiments.title: Clean test: 25% vs 35% human-game starts
experiments.what: Two identical training branches from round 40, differing only in the share of games started from people's games (25% or 35%).
experiments.why: E5 changed the rate while other things changed too, so it could not say which rate is better.
experiments.metric: 1,000 games head to head and the error on a fixed set of people's games.
experiments.result: Inconclusive: 35% won 505-495 (about ± 3%), error 0.6202 vs 0.6210. No change to production.

experiments.title: Targeted game starts and a final-road filter
experiments.what: Two offline tests: self-play started from chosen positions, and a search filter for the last road of longest road.
experiments.why: Both aimed at situations where the bot loses to people.
experiments.metric: 1,000 games each against the unchanged version.
experiments.result: Neither helped: targeted starts 485-515 (45-52%), road filter 472-528 (44-50%). Both stay off.

experiments.title: Warm starts and a looser promotion gate
experiments.what: Each round trains on from the previous round's net instead of from the best net; near misses in the promotion match get 2,000 more games.
experiments.why: Every round restarted from round 40, so small gains never added up.
experiments.metric: The best net's score against the round 13 anchor rising over rounds 57-62, and promotions.
experiments.result: No gain shown: rounds 57-62 scored 50.2-52.2%, none passed the gate (round 62: 50.3% ± 2.1%). Warm starts stay as the baseline.

experiments.title: Always take an immediate win
experiments.what: When the bot can win at once with a sure build or card, it plays that move, even if its policy rated the move low.
experiments.why: The search sometimes never looked at a winning move with a low prior (6 of 35 flagged positions).
experiments.metric: No missed immediate wins; at most 5% extra thinking time.
experiments.result: Shipped on the owner's word without an A/B test (taking a sure win can only win). Costs 0.25% of self-play time; took 6 wins in 8 test games.

experiments.title: A bigger net
experiments.what: Offline on the PC: a wider net (48,96 instead of 32,64) trained on the same data as a same-size control.
experiments.why: The net has about 100k weights and might be too small.
experiments.metric: Validation loss, wide vs control, then games at equal thinking time.
experiments.result: No difference (policy -0.0003). Both arms barely moved from their starting net, so this mostly measured a short fine-tune. Followed by E11b.

experiments.title: Bigger nets, trained longer
experiments.what: Three nets (normal, wider, deeper) trained 12 epochs at a higher learning rate on the same data.
experiments.why: To give a bigger net enough training to use its size.
experiments.metric: Validation loss; a gap of at least 0.005 before any games.
experiments.result: Every arm overfit, and wide and deep were within 0.001 of the normal net. The net is limited by data, not by size. Size unchanged.

experiments.title: Weight averaging
experiments.what: Each round's net is an average of its weights over the last part of training (as KataGo does).
experiments.why: New nets sat within noise of the best; averaging gives slightly stronger, steadier nets.
experiments.metric: Match scores and anchor of rounds 64-67 against rounds 59-63.
experiments.result: Ambiguous but not harmful: about 50.9% vs 50.7%, 2 promotions in 4 rounds vs 1 in 5. Stays on.

experiments.title: Self-play against a human-like opponent
experiments.what: In 15% of self-play games one seat plays like a person (moves sampled from the model of people's moves, no search).
experiments.why: The value net is too sure of late leads against people; games against human-style play should teach it.
experiments.metric: Late value bias on 623 live games (army + dev-card slice down 0.10), live value error, and no loss of strength.
experiments.result: No effect on the value (-0.006 ± 0.005 against round 73) and no cost to strength (49.5-49.9%). The seat played its dev cards like the net, not like people. Stays on as the base for E27.

experiments.title: Learn people's moves from the games they won
experiments.what: About 9% of the policy targets are moves people made in games they won against the bot.
experiments.why: People who beat the bot build fewer dead roads and more settlements.
experiments.metric: Over rounds 69-72: predicting people's moves, late value bias, self-play strength, and live play.
experiments.result: People's-move prediction up 8 points (55.2% to 63.2%); late value bias down 0.02 (real, a tenth of the gap); self-play strength equal. Stays on. Round 73, an E14 net, is live on all accounts since Oct 18, 2:16 AM. Final live check (Oct 18, 11:47 PM): round 73 went 235-165 (58.8%, 53.9-63.5%) over 400 ranked games against round 66's 216-149 (59.2%) over 365 on the same accounts: no live difference (-0.4 points, give or take 7), although round 73 beat round 66 in the self-play gate. Dead roads per game 2.12 vs 2.29.
experiments.next: Nothing. Closed.

experiments.title: Road Building's free roads get full thinking time
experiments.what: Fixed a bug: free roads from a Road Building card played before the dice roll got the 1-second dice budget instead of the normal 5 seconds.
experiments.why: 70% of the bot's Road Building plays were before the roll, so most free roads were barely searched.
experiments.metric: Free-road thinking time in the bots' logs, and dead roads per game not worse.
experiments.result: Free roads went from about 1.0 s / 800 searches to 4.4-4.5 s / 3,500-4,700. Dead roads 2.27 → 2.38 per game (difference +0.11 ± 0.30): no harm shown.

experiments.title: Value target mixes the game result with the search's value
experiments.what: Offline: nets trained with value targets that blend the final result with the search's estimate (0%, 30%, 50%, 100%).
experiments.why: The value loss is mostly noise from the final result; a smoother target might fix the live value error.
experiments.metric: Error on people's games down by at least 0.01, with no policy cost.
experiments.result: Real but tiny gain (at most 0.0012, ten times under the bar); the late overconfidence did not change. Not adopted.

experiments.title: Endgame filter toward a card- or trade-funded build
experiments.what: In the endgame, the search only considers moves on the path to a build paid for by Year of Plenty or trades.
experiments.why: In live games, the bot won more often when it always followed that path (+12-15 points, but confounded).
experiments.metric: Paired games, filter vs no filter: at least +1.5 points with the interval above 50%.
experiments.result: Filter lost: 47.8% ± 2.3% over 1,600 games. Not adopted; nothing deployed.

experiments.title: What is twice the search worth?
experiments.what: Round 66 played itself with twice the searches on one side: 2,400 vs 1,200, then 4,800 vs 2,400.
experiments.why: If more search wins clearly, bigger bot machines would be worth paying for.
experiments.metric: Win rate of the deeper side over 300-600 paired games per step.
experiments.result: About 1-2 points per doubling: 51.2% ± 3.8% (600 games) and 52.2% ± 4.1% (500 games). More search is not the lever; no bigger machines. Stopped by the owner.

experiments.title: Google Cloud spot machines for self-play
experiments.what: Cheap spot virtual machines in us-east1 play self-play games alongside the existing workers (about US$0.04-0.05 an hour each).
experiments.why: More games per round; the net is limited by data.
experiments.metric: Games per hour per machine, then the round's self-play time.
experiments.result: The 4-core machines play 776-830 games an hour each. us-central1 had no spot capacity (two machines lost within minutes), so the fleet moved to us-east1. Rounds 70-71 were not a clean test: they shared machines with a match and E18. Oct 20, 11:25 PM: closed, kept. The spot machines are now a standing part of the self-play fleet (nine in us-east1 and us-central1 tonight). A machine the cloud takes back is started again before the next round, and the loop hands its games to the others meanwhile.

experiments.title: The bot on the OpenHex bot ladder
experiments.what: Round 66 plays 1v1 on OpenHex, a public ladder of Catan bots, from its own small cloud machine (about US$1.8 a day).
experiments.why: A second, independent measure of strength against other bots.
experiments.metric: OpenHex Elo and win rate after 20 and 100 games.
experiments.result: First 20 games: no protocol errors on its own machine; 17 of 27 games won (63% ± 18%); Elo 1564, rank 8 of 21 (Oct 18, 2:20 AM). Round 66 final: 31 of 51 (61%), Elo 1573; round 73 plays since 9:24 AM. Oct 18, 11 AM: OpenHex uses plain random dice, not colonist's balanced dice (56 games, 4356 rolls), so the net plays with dice unlike its training. Oct 18, 11:15 AM: that costs no measurable strength: 1000 games of round 73 against itself on plain dice, the training-like dice input scored 51.2% ± 3.1%, so no client change. Oct 18, 11:55 AM: all 61 OpenHex boards lay the numbers in the official spiral, so a 6 never touches an 8 there; our self-play shuffles numbers, and 87% of its boards have a 6 next to an 8. The net has seen such boards, just rarely; no change. Closed Oct 20, 9:37 PM: the bot works and plays day and night. Round 73 won 66 of 121 (55%), 33-27 against catanrl-1v1-search, the ladder's main active bot. All games: 97 of 172 (56% ± 7%), Elo about 1576, rank 8 of 23.
experiments.next: Continued as E73, E86 and E87. The OpenHex line ended Oct 22, 10:05 PM (cloud credits used up); the closing note is in E87.

experiments.title: Round 152 on the OpenHex bot ladder
experiments.what: The OpenHex bot plays round 152 instead of round 73 (2,400 simulations, same machine), switched between games on the lead's call of 8:45 PM.
experiments.why: OpenHex is a ladder of other bots, not people. If round 152's self-play gain is real against bots, it should show here.
experiments.metric: Win rate over 100 round 152 games, overall and against catanrl-1v1-search, compared with round 73's 55% (33-27 against that bot).
experiments.result: Oct 22, 6:35 AM, verdict at 100 games: round 152 won 52 (52% ± 10%), above the 46% revert line, so it is kept until the switch. Moving first 26-19, moving second 26-29. Against catanrl-1v1-search 46-41 (first 22-13, second 24-28), the same as round 73 seat for seat (first 20-12, second 13-15). Against the rank-1 bot hexn-4d.0 3-6. Round 73 had 56% over 172, so round 152 is no better on OpenHex. Elo 1511, rank 12 of 23.
experiments.next: Closed. E86 (E54's step 50) takes over at the end of the current game.

experiments.title: A newer net pinned on one account
experiments.what: Planned: bot7 would play round 69 (an E14 net) while the others stayed on round 66.
experiments.why: Only live games show whether E14 helps against people.
experiments.metric: bot7's win rate over 200 games against the other accounts over the same hours.
experiments.result: Closed without deploying: round 73, itself an E14 net, was promoted and went live everywhere, so a pin would measure nothing. First live reading, round 73 vs 66: 60.4% ± 8.3 (134 games) vs 58.5% (393). Inside the noise.

experiments.title: Self-play machines in the owner's trial project
experiments.what: Nine 4-core machines in the owner's free-trial Google Cloud project play self-play, paid from the trial credit (about US$37 a day).
experiments.why: More self-play games per round.
experiments.metric: Seconds per game and the round's self-play time.
experiments.result: The six machines outside the match play 7.7-9.8 s per game per process. The credit runs out around Oct 25. Oct 20, 11:25 PM: closed, kept. All nine machines still play self-play as part of the fleet; the test is answered. Oct 21, 9:20 AM: the nine play 42-46% of every round's self-play (rounds 165-185). Training's GPU machine is in the same project. Estimated spend so far about US$140 of US$300; together they burn about US$42 a day, so the credit ends around Oct 25 and the GPU machine stops with it.
experiments.next: The owner chose (Oct 21, 9:09 AM): keep the nine until about US$40 is left, then delete them so the GPU machine runs about a week longer. Planned deletion: Oct 24, about 6 AM Toronto. Training drops to 3,400 games a round from then.

experiments.title: More weight on people's games for the value net
experiments.what: Offline: people's games repeated 16 or 32 times in training (now 4), against a repeat of the current setting.
experiments.why: The value net is too sure of late leads against people, and people's games are only about 10% of what it learns from.
experiments.metric: Late bias down at least 0.03 and error on people's games down at least 0.005, with no policy cost.
experiments.result: Failed, nothing deployed. On 619 people's games, against the repeat-4 rerun: 16x lowered the late bias by 0.020 and the error by 0.002; 32x lowered the bias by 0.030 but the error not at all (within noise). The bar needed both. The live net (round 73) already has a lower error (by 0.007) than every arm. More weight on people's games is not the fix for the late gap.
experiments.next: Nothing. People's games stay at 4x. The GPU is free for E40 when the lead says go. Earlier: launched by the lead Oct 18, 2:45 PM (job e23, pid 1224833). Three arms on the PC's GPU, each started in the first 2 minutes of a round's match; the loop now waits for the GPU instead of training on the CPU. About 15 min per arm, so results around 5 to 6 PM; the training workstream scores them (long_games.py and calibrate on the human holdout) and reports the verdict. Oct 18, 4:10 PM preview (h16 and h32 done, h4 not yet), against the older repeat-4 net: 16x lowers the late bias by 0.017 and the error by 0.002; 32x by 0.027 and 0.002. Neither meets the bar. The live net (round 73) already has a lower error than both. Final verdict once h4 is in, about 5 PM.

experiments.title: Two training-loop speedups
experiments.what: A round whose self-play already finished skips its preparation steps, and idle machines take a failed machine's games at once.
experiments.why: Round 70 lost 19 minutes between its verdict and the next training.
experiments.metric: Time from a round's verdict to the next training.
experiments.result: 8 seconds in rounds 72 and 73 (round 70: 19 min). Works.

experiments.title: The coordinator's own self-play as a job, with a smaller share
experiments.what: The main machine plays its self-play share like any other worker, and that share is much smaller (64 games instead of 256).
experiments.why: Round 72's self-play waited 30 of its 37 minutes on the busy main machine while six machines sat idle.
experiments.metric: Self-play time of rounds 73-74 against round 72's 37 min.
experiments.result: Works, kept (closed Oct 20, 11:25 PM). Round 74's self-play took 8.3 minutes against round 72's 37, and idle machines took other hosts' games while the main machine played.

experiments.title: A shorter self-play tail
experiments.what: The last batch of games is split across all of a machine's processes, and an idle fast machine also plays a slow machine's last batch.
experiments.why: Rounds 75-77 waited on one slow batch at the end of self-play.
experiments.metric: Self-play time, against 17.5-20.5 min.
experiments.result: Round 80: 14.1 min of play (rounds 75-77: about 16-17). Better, a little short of the 12-13 hoped for. Kept.

experiments.title: The human-like seat holds its knights like people
experiments.what: The human-like self-play seat (E13) is nudged to hold its action cards, so it ends with about as many at turn 60+ as people do.
experiments.why: People sitting on knights late is where the value net is most overconfident, and self-play never showed it.
experiments.metric: After 3 full rounds (79-81): late army + dev-card bias paired against round 73 (-0.10 to adopt, -0.03 is a real signal); live late value error under 0.426; match score at least about 49%.
experiments.result: No effect, kept on because it costs nothing. Late overconfidence went down by only 0.019, 0.019 and 0.015 in rounds 79-81 (a real signal needs 0.03). Late value error stayed at 0.42; match scores 50.3%, 51.0% and 49.3%.

experiments.title: Prepare all worker machines at once
experiments.what: The copying of code and nets to the 22 worker machines runs in parallel instead of one after another.
experiments.why: Preparing them one by one took 3 min 20 s every round.
experiments.metric: Preparation time under 30 s; match time per 1,000 games.
experiments.result: Works, kept (closed Oct 20, 11:25 PM). Preparing the machines took 24 seconds in round 81, against about 3 minutes before (3 min 2 s and 3 min 30 s in round 74).

experiments.title: Split the promotion match by machine speed
experiments.what: The promotion match's games are split between machines by measured speed, not by process count.
experiments.why: Fast machines sat idle while the slow ones finished.
experiments.metric: Minutes per 1,000 match games (round 78: 13.6-15.8).
experiments.result: Round 79's 4,000-game match took 26.4 min: 6.6 min per 1,000 games, about 2.2 times faster. Kept.

experiments.title: Later match batches split by measured match speed
experiments.what: After a match's first batch, games are split by each machine's measured match speed, not its self-play speed.
experiments.why: Self-play speed is a rough guide: the last 2,000 games of round 79 waited 774 s on the slowest machine against 610 s for an even split.
experiments.metric: Minutes per 1,000 match games (round 79: 6.6), expect about 5.5; verdict after two matches.
experiments.result: Works, kept. Went live with E32 at round 81. Now it only sizes the coordinator's own share: 14 games in the first batch, 47 in the second once its speed was measured. Together with E32: 6.6 to 4.8 min per 1,000 games.

experiments.title: One training pass per round instead of four
experiments.what: Each round trains once over its data instead of four times.
experiments.why: The validation loss stops improving after the first pass in every round 72-80; the later passes only memorise. Our data is reused 18-24 times against KataGo's 4.
experiments.metric: Over 3 rounds: same validation loss, match score at least the 50.2% of rounds 74-79, live value error no worse, and about 9 min less training per round.
experiments.result: No change in strength, but faster. Rounds 82-84 scored 49.2% over 5,000 games against round 73, the same as the 50.2% of the four-pass rounds. Validation loss the same. Training takes 3 min instead of 12, so a round is about 13 min instead of 22. Live value error 0.579 (was 0.575), with the late game creeping up: 0.424, 0.426, 0.430. Kept.
experiments.next: Oct 18, 2:20 PM: the late-game live error reached 0.440 (rounds 90-93 climbed 0.435, 0.438, 0.439, 0.440), so training goes to two passes from round 95. Round 73, the live net, still measures 0.420 on the same games, so the newer nets drifted; the games did not get harder. Nothing live changed. If rounds 95-97 still climb, try four passes.

experiments.title: Match games as a queue the machines draw from
experiments.what: Instead of a fixed split, each machine takes the next match game whenever one of its processes is free.
experiments.why: Any fixed split leaves a 15-20% tail; even identical machines took 283-372 s for the same games.
experiments.metric: All machines finish within about one game of each other; about 5.3-5.5 min per 1,000 games against 6.6-6.8. Two rounds.
experiments.result: Works, kept. Round 81's match: 4.9 and 4.8 min per 1,000 games (round 80: 6.8). All 22 worker machines finished within 262-298 s of the start (round 80: 113-407 s). Since Oct 17: 14-16 min per 1,000 games down to 4.8, about 3x faster.
experiments.next: Self-play is now about as long as a round, so it is the next bottleneck.

experiments.title: Self-play games as a queue the machines draw from
experiments.what: Self-play is cut into small 8-game pieces. Each machine, the main one included, takes the next piece whenever one of its processes is free, like the match games in E32.
experiments.why: Self-play is now about as long as a whole round. Round 82 took 13.1 min for 5,000 games and waited about 2.3 min at the end for the last machines. Machine speeds vary from round to round, so a fixed split can't fix that.
experiments.metric: Minutes of self-play per 5,000 games, and all machines finishing within a few minutes of each other. Before: 13.1 min. Two rounds.
experiments.result: So far, 2 rounds: the queue works. Rounds 85 and 86 took 16.4 and 17.9 min, with a match running on the same machines the whole time. All machines finished within 41 s of each other (before: 2.3 min). Games have been about 55% slower per machine since round 83, before this change, because self-play now overlaps the match, so 13.1 min is no longer a fair comparison. A bug made the main machine's own self-play hang when told to stop. It cost no round time, but left processes behind. Fixed and live from 11:07 AM. Rounds 87 and 88 (Oct 18, 12:10 PM): 18.1 and 18.8 min, all machines within 1.5-2 min of each other, and self-play ends 2 s after its last piece. A whole round takes 21-22 min, the same or a little better than before (21-24 min). Works, kept: the gain is no waiting on slow machines and no lost games, not raw speed.
experiments.next: Closed. Self-play and the match share the same machines, so the next gain must come from faster games themselves.

experiments.title: OpenHex dice: plain dice from the first roll
experiments.what: OpenHex's rules page says 1v1 uses balanced dice, but the rolls don't behave like a 36-card deck. The bot now treats them as plain dice from the first roll, instead of switching after the first roll a deck can't make (about the 8th).
experiments.why: In all 56 saved games some roll is impossible for colonist's deck, and how uneven each game's rolls are matches plain dice (9.5 vs 9.9 for plain dice, 3.4 for balanced). The games' own data also says balanced, so either the site's balancing is much weaker than colonist's or it doesn't work. The site describes no algorithm and lists no contact. Our net only ever trained on balanced dice, so we also checked whether that costs strength.
experiments.metric: Round 73 on plain dice, the input the bot gives the net vs a balanced-looking input, 1000 games without search.
experiments.result: No cost: the balanced-looking input scored 51.2% ± 3.1% over 1000 games, so the plain-dice input costs under about 3% even with no search. The bot keeps its dice input and now uses plain odds from the first roll. Live on the OpenHex machine after its current game.
experiments.next: Nothing. Revert: git revert the commit and push to the OpenHex machine.

experiments.title: Self-play on colonist's real number layout
experiments.what: Self-play and the match use colonist's fixed number spiral instead of random numbers. Live since Oct 18, 3:00 PM; round 97 is the first round on these boards.
experiments.why: All 228 colonist boards we recorded use the standard spiral, so a 6 never touches an 8 and equal numbers never touch. Our self-play has a 6 next to an 8 on 86% of boards. 65% of self-play games and every match game are on boards the live bots never see. Checked the rest of the board too (4,279 colonist boards, Oct 18, 11:55 AM): ports and resource tiles already match ours, so the numbers are the only difference.
experiments.metric: Live value error (now 0.579) over 3 rounds, match score no worse, then live wins if a net is promoted.
experiments.result: Rounds 99-101 against rounds 91-93, live error by phase: opening 0.890 vs 0.889 (same), middle 0.506 vs 0.509, late 0.427 vs 0.440 (better). Overall 0.578-0.581, was 0.584. Match scores 47-50%, no worse than before, but no promotion yet. Two other changes landed in the same rounds (training from the best net, back to 2 passes), so the gain can't be credited to the spiral alone.
experiments.next: Kept. If a net passes the match but narrowly fails the round-13 check, re-measure that check on the new boards first.

experiments.title: Self-play keeps 32 games going per process
experiments.what: Each self-play process used to play 8 games at a time, and near the end of each 8 the network worked on only a game or two. Now each process keeps up to 32 games going and starts new ones as games end.
experiments.why: Bigger network batches cost less per game. On 64 test games: 14.91 s a game before, 13.82 after (7.3% faster). The games are the same, move for move.
experiments.metric: Self-play minutes per round for rounds 99-101, compared with rounds 87-94 (5,000 games in 18.5 min on average, last few games taking about 0.6 min). Also watch the end of each round and worker memory.
experiments.result: Round 96 (3:15 PM): each 4-core VM played 30% faster, but the round took 21.2 min instead of 18.5. Machines started second copies of games other busy machines were already holding, so 6,640 games were played for 5,000. Fixed at 3:55 PM: a machine now copies another's games only when it is nearly out of work. Round 98 (4:15 PM), the first round with the fix: 5,216 games played for 5,000 (7,024 in round 97), and self-play took 15.4 min, 17% less than the old 18.5, even with two VMs missing. Kept at 6:10 PM: over rounds 98-102 self-play took 11.0-15.8 min (14.2 on average, 23% less than 18.5), with 5,176-5,624 games played for 5,000. The few extra games are mostly re-plays of work a preempted VM dropped.
experiments.next: Nothing; done. Revert if ever needed: git revert both commits; it takes effect next round.

experiments.title: Train on the last 18 rounds instead of the last 6

experiments.title: Why nets after round 73 judge the late game against people worse
experiments.what: A check, no training and no games: measure the error on people's games for 15 production nets from round 60 to round 115.
experiments.why: Three fixes (the value target, more weight on people's games, a smaller learning rate) all failed to keep round 73's late-game accuracy against people (0.409; every newer net is 0.42-0.43). Either round 73 was a lucky round, or the newer self-play data drifts away from how people play late.
experiments.metric: Late-game error on people's games (648 games) by round. Round 73 alone below its neighbours means luck; a steady climb means drift, and the next step compares the late game in old and new self-play data.
experiments.result: Round 73 is not a lucky outlier: rounds 70 to 80 all sit at 0.404-0.409, rounds 85 and later at 0.412-0.423. The self-play data does not drift: a late lead converts in self-play as often in round 112 as in round 58. Scaling the net's late values down gains nothing (0.408 stays 0.408), and every net ranks late positions the same. Round 73 and round 66 differ by 0.012 here yet win the same share live, so this error is not where the Elo is.
experiments.next: No value shrink and no target change. The real gap is that people come back from late leads more than self-play opponents do; the lever would be self-play that plays more like people late, not a new loss.

experiments.title: Late-game starts from people's games, with the human-style seat playing the person's side
experiments.what: A design, not built. Self-play games that start from real games against people at turns 60-100, with the human-style opponent model playing the person's side from there on, so the net sees people-like late comebacks.
experiments.why: People come back from late leads more than self-play opponents do. The human-style seat already in production (E13, E27) starts from an empty board, loses 78-88% of its games and rarely reaches a close late position; real-game starts stop at turn 60 and are then played by the net on both sides.
experiments.metric: Late-game error on people's games against a control trained the same way without these games: must drop by 0.010 or more. Then the usual gate against round 73 (2,000 games, 52% passes).
experiments.next: Recommended not to build yet: a 0.01 late-error gap made no visible difference live (round 66 and round 73 win 59% each), so even success may not add Elo. Waiting for live-loss's win rate by opponent rating to show where the missing strength is.

experiments.title: Self-play full searches at 800 simulations instead of 400

The loop sits at a fixed point: round 73 trained on its own search's output gives round 73 back. In AlphaZero-style loops the gain per round is how much the search improves on the net, and E18 showed a doubling of simulations is worth 1-2 points here. The self-play fleet finishes its 5,000 games in about 14 minutes while training and the match take about 33, so thinking twice as long costs no wall-clock.

Training plus match takes 24 minutes when the match stops early and 40-45 when it runs on, so self-play now sets the pace only in short rounds, by about 3-7 minutes. The gate verdict comes at rounds 133-138. Gates so far (Oct 19, 2:45 PM): rounds 125-129 scored 49.7%, 51.0%, 49.4%, 50.7% and 49.8% against round 73, no promotion. First reading at 9 PM from rounds 125-132. Two spot VMs were lent to E54 at 3:11 PM (up to 5 hours; round 132 is the first round without them). Self-play is about 8% slower meanwhile and those rounds don't count toward the time limit. Both came back at 4:56 PM, so round 133 is the last round without them and rounds 134-138 have the full fleet. First reading (lead, Oct 19, 9 PM): rounds 125-132 pooled 50.15% against round 73 over 45,000 games (± 0.5), against 49.9% before the change: no effect yet. The verdict rounds so far: 133 at 50.0% (8,000), 134 at 50.7% (8,000), 135 at 47.5% (1,000), pooled 50.2%. VERDICT (training, Oct 19, 11:35 PM): rounds 133-138 scored 50.0% (8,000), 50.7% (8,000), 47.5% (1,000), 50.8% (8,000), 50.25% (8,000) and 49.9% (8,000) against round 73. Pooled: 50.27% over 41,000 games (± 0.5), against 49.9% before. Under the 51% bar, and level with rounds 125-132 (50.15%). Twice the thinking in self-play did not make a stronger net. No promotion in 14 rounds. Live error held: round 138 at 0.570 overall (opening 0.889, middle 0.497, late 0.403), against 0.577 / 0.410 late before.
experiments.next: Closed (Oct 19, 11:35 PM): back to 400 simulations in the training settings, with the same safe restart that starts E59. experiments.what: A plan, offline first. Self-play's move target is the search's improved policy: the net's own move odds sharpened by how good each move looked in the search. The sharpening scale is fixed at 1 (c_scale). At a 400-simulation search that scale turns a tiny difference in two moves' search values (a few hundredths) into an almost all-or-nothing target. Try scales of 0.5, 0.25 and 0.1 for the stored target only; the search itself is unchanged.
experiments.why: Research measured (Oct 19) that two 400-simulation searches of the same position pick a different top move 1 time in 10, with almost all-or-nothing targets that flip. The net cannot fit targets that contradict each other, so it learns a blur and stays where it is (round 73 still differs from its own targets by 0.41 nats after training on them). A softer target that keeps the ranking of the moves but not the false certainty should be easier to learn. Source: Danihelka et al. 2022, Policy improvement by planning with Gumbel (ICLR), where this scale is a free parameter; and KataGo, whose move target at a few hundred playouts is the visit distribution, softer than ours.
experiments.metric: Offline, on the same positions: how often two independent searches' targets disagree on the top move and their distance (KL) at each scale, and how far each target sits from the net's prior (too close means nothing to learn). A scale that cuts the disagreement by half while keeping most of the distance from the prior goes to a production trial after E51's verdict (the usual gate over 6 rounds against the 49.9% baseline).

experiments.title: Does the robber take more from the bot than from the person in long games?
experiments.started: Oct 21, 8:50 AM: the lead's research item, from E70 and E71's numbers; live-loss measures it from the captures.
experiments.what: Over the 2100+ games with converted captures (E71's 1,582 games), at every roll from turn 20 to the end: each side's expected income a roll from all its buildings (pips, cities doubled), the share of that income the robber is blocking, the share of income on its single best hex, and the number of distinct hexes it draws from. experiments.why: People keep 0.4-0.7 more settlements than the bot whether they win or lose (E71), our openings lean ore+wheat and away from wood+brick (E72 part 2), and the bot wins short games (67 rolls) but loses long ones (83 rolls). If the bot's income is more concentrated and more often blocked than the person's, that is a concrete mechanism for the late losses, and one self-play opponents do not punish because they build the same way. experiments.metric: Relative income blocked by the robber, bot vs person, in 90+ roll games the bot lost, with 95% ranges; the concentration of income on the best hex; distinct hexes. A gap of 10% or more relative (bot more blocked) with the range excluding zero means the mechanism is real and goes to research (a self-play check: the net's value error on positions where its best hex is robbed) and to live-play (a robber-move check). No gap means the settlement count is style, and the lead looks elsewhere.

experiments.title: Does the net see a thin Longest Road lead slipping away? (study)
experiments.status: done (Oct 21, 3:55 PM): not blind to the road; the net is too sure late in every road state
experiments.what: From the captured games against 2100+ players, take every position where the bot holds Longest Road by 1 or 2 roads at roll 60 in a game that ran 70+ rolls. Compare the net's stated win chance there with what happened, split by whether the bot kept the road, and against the same positions where the holder leads by 3 or more. Then the same at the moment the road is lost: how much the net's value drops versus the real 2-point swing.
experiments.why: Live-loss (Oct 21, 2:20 PM): in long games the bot keeps a 1-2 road lead only 32-37% of the time, people keep theirs 88-92% (1,639 games); Largest Army shows no gap. Building the road at once does not fix it (playouts, 2:30 PM: worth at most 2-3 points), so the fault is likely in how the value prices the threat over several turns, or in where the roads go. If the net rates a margin-1 lead like a margin-3 lead, it is blind to the race, and a training target (who holds the road at the end, or the opponent's reach) is the fix; if it sees the threat and still plays elsewhere, the fix is in search or in live-play's plans.
experiments.metric: Calibration gap: stated minus realized win chance for margin 1-2 holders, versus margin 3+ holders, with 95% ranges; and the value drop at the loss of the road versus the realized swing. A gap of 10 points or more for thin leads, not present for wide ones, means blind.
experiments.result: 1,077 live games vs 2100+ that ran 70+ rolls, the best net (round 189) at the bot's roll 60-63. Bot holds the road by 1-2: the net says 56.0%, the bot won 39.3%, too sure by 16.7 points (95% range 11.6 to 22.1; 214 games). Bot holds by 3+: says 67.4%, won 52.4%, too sure by 15.0 (10.6 to 20.0; 252). Nobody holds: too sure by 14.2 (9.8 to 19.2; 234). So the gap for thin leads is there, but the same gap is there for wide leads and with no road at all: it is the known late overconfidence, not a blind spot for the road race. The net does price a thin lead lower (56% vs 67%). When the bot loses the road after roll 60 (335 games), its value drops 13.0 points (11.2 to 14.8) and it still says 41.2% while it wins 28.1%. One road-specific hint: when the person holds a thin lead, the net is too sure by 13.8 (8.9 to 19.2) vs 6.0 (1.6 to 10.8) when the person's lead is wide; people keep thin leads 80% of the time and the net seems to expect to take the road back. Verdict by the rule: not blind (the gap is not specific to thin leads). A Longest Road target is not supported; the lever is the general late-game value target (research's task 3).

experiments.next: The road play itself (where the roads go, the chaser's race) goes to live-play and live-loss. Research folds the late overconfidence (about 14-17 points at roll 60 against 2100+) into its late-game target proposal.

experiments.title: The person's chair played by the people model from people's late positions
experiments.status: closed: dead (the people model is an easier opponent than the net, on round 73 and again on step 50)

E84 showed the net over-rates the bot's chair and under-rates the person's in positions people steer into, and that self-play labels from those positions cannot correct it (self-play is calibrated against itself, +0.1). The live labels differ because people play the person's chair differently from the net. A people-like opponent in that chair may give labels closer to live without more live games, the way AlphaStar's league used human-data agents to give its self-play what self-play alone lacked (Vinyals et al., Nature 2019).

If the bot's chair wins as much or more, the idea is dead in one match.
